assumptions: Scaled-workload (fixed-time) premise: problem size grows with N so the parallel part scales; serial fraction s is measured on the parallel system and stays fixed as N grows.
s + p = 1 by definition (serial plus parallel time fractions on the parallel system, normalized T = 1).
Ideal linear scaling of the parallel part; overheads excluded.
models.inverse_notes: p = (S-s)/N needs N != 0 (guarded N>=1); s = S-p*N needs p,N. Check: S=9.1,p=0.9,N=10 gives s=0.1. N=1 gives S=s+p=1 under the s+p=1 premise (checked). Algebraic only; does not test the fixed-time premise.
limitations: Fixed-time/scaled-workload premise only; fixed-workload bounds use Amdahl (b01), not this record.
Excludes communication/synchronization overhead and serial growth with scale.
N is a processor count (positive integer); fractional N has no meaning.

references.method: Ordinary case: serial 0.1 plus 0.9x10 = 9.1. Synthetic, materially larger scale than the 4-processor case.
references.provenance: Independent arithmetic check with synthetic inputs.
Independent arithmetic check with synthetic inputs.

references.method: Limiting identity: one processor gives no scaled speedup (s+p = 1).

rejection_cases.reason: Parallel fraction p is an asserted input; omitting it leaves S undetermined.

relationship.locator: Definition section: S = s + p x N with s + p = 1, normalized T = 1 derivation showing serial baseline s and scaled parallel part Np.
relationship.original_equation: S = s + p x N = s + (1 - s) x N (scaled speedup with s + p = 1)
relationship.translation_notes: Locals s, p, N; output S. Dimensionless fractions times processor count give dimensionless scaled speedup.

sources.evidence: Gives scaled speedup S = s + pN with s + p = 1, the N-processor linear model, and the T = 1 normalization derivation (serial part s, parallel part Np on the serial baseline).

models.inverse_notes: S = E*N needs E,N; N = S/E needs E != 0. Check: E=0.91,N=10 gives S=9.1. N=0 excluded. Super-linear E>1 admissible.
limitations: Super-linear speedup (E > 1, e.g. cache effects) is admissible, not an error; typical [0,1] is descriptive.
Efficiency alone does not diagnose bottlenecks; pair with Amdahl/Gustafson fractions.
